name: Radio manual
description: A dog-eared operator's manual. The Morse table is on page 12.
text:

Morse: a dot is short, a dash is three times longer. Short gap between letters, long gap between words.

name: Decoder card
description: A cardboard decoder from a cereal box. The alphabet, written forwards and backwards.
text:
SECRET AGENT DECODER — mirror code!

A B C D E F G H I J K L M
Z Y X W V U T S R Q P O N

Every letter becomes its mirror: A↔Z, B↔Y, C↔X… Use it twice and you're back where you started.

name: Cell wall chart
description: A grid scratched into a holding cell wall, copied onto paper.
text:
Scratched into the wall of cell 2:

    1 2 3 4 5
 1  A B C D E
 2  F G H I J
 3  L M N O P
 4  Q R S T U
 5  V W X Y Z

(C and K share a square.)
Knock the row, pause, knock the column. ·· ··· is row 2, column 3: H.

name: Puzzle notebook
description: Someone's notebook of word games. Half of it is about one cipher.
text:
VIGENÈRE — the 'unbreakable' one (it isn't).

Pick a keyword. Write it over the message, repeating it. Shift each letter by its keyword letter (A=0, B=1… Z=25).

To decode: shift back. Without the keyword you're lost, so whoever sends these always leaves a hint.

My favourite keywords are things everybody knows but nobody says.

name: Programmer's notebook
description: A notebook from an IT office: tables, scribbles, coffee rings.
text:
BASE 64 — for when you have to send bytes through something that only takes letters.

A–Z = 0–25 · a–z = 26–51 · 0–9 = 52–61 · + = 62 · / = 63

Every 4 characters are 3 letters of the original. '=' at the end is padding.

'SGVsbG8=' → Hello. Don't ask me why I know this by heart.

name: Pad page 7
description: A page of five-digit groups headed 'PAD 7'. Burn after use. Nobody did.
text:
ONE-TIME PAD — PAGE 7

12930 48211 70533 91847 26519 30772 85106 44398 61025 79314

Subtract each pair of digits from the message, without borrowing. 01=A … 26=Z, 00=space.

name: Field radio handbook
description: A 1974 field radio handbook. Words underlined in pencil, page after page.
text:
FIELD RADIO HANDBOOK (1974), the underlined bits.

— page 1 —
1  Chapter one: the field radio
2  Keep the antenna dry and do not answer every voice
3  A good operator listens more than talks
— page 2 —
1  Repeaters work best under clear skies
2  Echo returns from the dam on the long band
3  Seven words is enough for a message
— page 3 —
1  Some stations transmit lies on purpose
2  Learn them, log them, never trust them

Book codes give page-line-word: find the page, count the lines, count the words.
